reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / standard orthopaedic oncology texts
clinicalPearls: The rarest of the benign cartilage tumours, typically presenting in adolescents and young adults with slowly progressive localised pain and sometimes swelling
Has a predilection for the metaphysis of long bones, classically the proximal tibia, and also occurs in flat bones and small bones of the foot
Radiographs show an eccentric, lobulated, well-defined lytic metaphyseal lesion with a sclerotic scalloped margin, often expanding the cortex
In contrast to many cartilage tumours it usually shows little or no visible matrix calcification on imaging
Histology reveals lobules of spindle and stellate cells in a myxoid and chondroid background with peripheral hypercellularity and giant cells
The hypercellular, myxoid appearance can be mistaken for chondrosarcoma, so clinicopathological correlation is essential
Treatment is surgical, usually curettage with bone grafting, reserving wider excision for recurrent or aggressive lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Chondromyxoid fibroma is a benign neoplasm derived from cartilage-forming mesenchyme, characterised by lobules of stellate and spindle-shaped cells embedded in an abundant myxoid and chondroid matrix, with increased cellularity and scattered giant cells at the lobule margins. It typically arises in the metaphysis of tubular bones and grows in an eccentric, expansile fashion that thins and remodels the overlying cortex. Recurrent rearrangements involving the GRM1 gene have been described as a driver of the tumour. Despite its sometimes worrying microscopic hypercellularity and pleomorphism, its behaviour is benign, and the main clinical difficulty is distinguishing it from chondrosarcoma.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing an eccentric lobulated lytic metaphyseal lesion with a sclerotic margin
CT to assess cortical thinning, expansion and any subtle matrix
MRI to define the lobulated architecture and soft-tissue extent
Image-guided or open biopsy with expert bone pathology review
Molecular studies for GRM1 rearrangement where available
Staging imaging if malignancy cannot be excluded on initial assessment
redFlags: Rapid growth, cortical breakthrough or a soft-tissue mass suggesting chondrosarcoma
Markedly atypical histology that cannot confidently be called benign
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is favourable, with cure expected after complete curettage or excision, although local recurrence is recognised, particularly after incomplete removal in younger patients. Malignant transformation is very rare.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing chondrosarcoma because of the hypercellular, myxoid histology
Underestimating the recurrence risk after simple curettage in adolescents
Failing to correlate imaging with pathology in an equivocal cartilage lesion
Missing a pathological fracture arising through a cortically thinned lesion
